The studio archive holds eighty-seven HIV and STD prevention campaigns. Three stand for them here: a CDC national testing campaign, a franchise that has run for more than two decades, and PrEP outreach in Ohio.

Four campaigns, one argument: older kids in the foster system need families, and the families are already out there. San Francisco, Alameda County, Detroit, and a national run for the Human Rights Campaign.
One county health system kept coming back: fentanyl harm reduction for users, primary prevention for teens — four campaigns, ages twelve to thirty-nine, each in its own register.
For the International Network of People Who Use Drugs: posters aimed at United Nations policy makers, for drug law built on evidence, human rights, and dignity. American Graphic Design Award, 2009.
Flood-risk awareness for Santa Clara County, in four languages. Communicator Gold, and NAFSMA first place for public flood awareness, 2019.
A juice box with teeth. Sugary drinks and childhood obesity, argued to parents of under-fives in Contra Costa County. Communicator Gold for the campaign site, and a published evaluation.

IDNYC put a free municipal ID within reach of every New Yorker; One County One Future told Santa Clara County's immigrants, in five languages, that the county stood with them. Both took Communicator Awards.
Smoking cessation for Chicago's LGBTQ women of color: pride and smoking don't go together. American Graphic Design Award, 2014.
NSCAD under Ehses, Brooks, and Scharfe. Design as argument, not decoration. Typography, grids, the rhetorical structures that hold language in place.
Public health, civic engagement, human rights. Applied rhetoric — logos, pathos, ethos deployed in the one domain where getting the message wrong carries human cost.
The Farallones colony. Mor, a foggy tour through beauty and its undoing. A year of solo shows at Slowbender Gallery. Light as a medium of meaning.
One line between two trees. A San Francisco record. sfslackline.org, built because the same questions kept coming. Physical balance as practice and metaphor.
Architectural drawings to foundation dig to cantilevered reading nook. The need to make something outside the digital realm, with your own hands, to scale.
DYork Music. Guitar, vocals, a kit at fifty-one. More unfinished songs than finished ones. The search for rhythm in a life of rearranged rooms.
The Forge. Hampton. Typeset.us — a turn-of-the-millennium thesis finally completed. repodrum. The God Show. The current synthesis of rhetoric, typography, and infrastructure.
Twelve years in kitchens. Twenty years at one agency. The real work lives in years five through fifteen.

The post was in the ground first — an old San Francisco pier piling set in rebar and concrete, engineered for the 3,300-pound pull of a slackline. Then a year when my son was five and the rest of the world felt heavier than usual. I built a house around the post that was already holding the line.

A submerged ridge, granite peaks breaking the waterline where the continental shelf drops six thousand feet. Three hundred thousand seabirds, great whites in fall, Roosevelt’s 1909 refuge. Four years of photographs. Eighteen prints. One gallery year.
Dolores Park, 2009. A blond stranger walking a line between two palms. By year one, rigging my own. By year five, sfslackline.org was the container the questions kept asking to be put into.
Print solved line-breaking in 1981. The browser never did. A quarter-century gap between diagnosis and tool, closed in collaboration with a language model that knows the literature.
Jennifer Hampton held the agency’s institutional memory. After she was gone, a software version: thirteen state portals, a profile that learns, a scoring floor below which nothing reaches a human.
How to reconcile a peak human experience in nature with the ongoing human role in its undoing.

The second Slowbender show. A foggy tour through the paradox of peak human experience in nature and our role in its ongoing destruction. Coastal beauty that lures you in and leaves you wondering at your own blood on the beach.
Hanno Ehses had studied under Otl Aicher. He co-authored the Rhetorical Handbook with Ellen Lupton. What he gave me at NSCAD was not a style. It was an engine.

Les Pappas built Better World Advertising to take only the work that mattered. Twenty years of HIV prevention, civic engagement, behavior change. The theory became practice. The practice became the life.
Short songs for the streaming era. Rooted in the Maritime indie scene of Halifax youth; influenced by Townes Van Zandt, Lou Reed, Alex Maas, and Jackie Mittoo. Raw, unpredictable, specific.
Some songs are about a thing. This one is about the shape of the thing — the slow work of finding a rhythm that is yours when you arrived inside a family you did not choose.

I bought a second-hand kit because my son had been talking about forming a rock band. Then I realized I kinda suck at drums. So I built the tool I wish I had had at thirteen, when my own kit lived in somebody else’s basement.
Ask any question. Eleven belief systems answer in parallel. Over time, your votes produce a philosophical DNA — which traditions speak to you, not the ones you think should.
A richer life compounds the way money does — quietly, daily, in the things you do not skip.

Two words that belong together if you let them. Wellth — wealth and wellness as one daily habit, paired tips you cannot skip, a streak that adds up. Built in Expo through 2025 and 2026, with end-to-end encryption, Supabase auth, a dignified owl, and gold serif type holding the whole thing together.

AI portrait generation as a curated kit: lens, wardrobe, lighting, backdrop chosen from controlled catalogs, run through Gemini and GPT-image. Standard and Pro tiers, a credit ledger, API keys. The clean-room v2 rebuilt on Next.js 16 after the original at ebaix proved the idea worked.

A private collection of the world’s most exceptional properties, each photographed once and then unfolded into the rooms they could be — without losing the rooms they are. Three directions per listing, in seven languages, indexed and discoverable. Architectural fidelity is the rule, not a feature.

A circular arcade space defender. Your ship orbits Earth as a guardian; auto-firing cannons handle the threats; the player rotates to face waves of invaders. Pixel art, mobile and desktop, in a single HTML file with no dependencies. A small argument that the web still works.

San Francisco quietly dropped the speed limit on its automated camera streets from thirty to twenty-five — a trap, in practice, for the forgetful driver on the routine commute. The answer was a PWA: thirty-three cameras, GPS, geofenced approaches, and a strange British woman warning you about each one in turn.

A multi-voice rewriting tool for advertising work. Five distinct editorial channels — Editorial Restraint, Lyrical Depth, Minimal Authority, Intellectual Clarity, Human Persuasion — generated in parallel, rated and highlighted at the phrase level, then synthesized into one Authorized Version. The way a copy meeting actually goes, only faster.

Mono in, stereo out. A fixed signal chain — dynamics, drive, character, stereo, space, output — five macros (Touch, Heat, Motion, Depth, Body), and an AI that watches how you turn the knobs without ever touching the audio. Pedalboard format, fully analog signal path. Built for the set, not the museum.

Typography is the art and technique of arranging type to make written language legible, readable and appealing.
Good typography enhances the reading experience and helps communicate your message effectively to your audience.
It creates hierarchy, harmony, and helps guide the reader through your content in a meaningful way.
Small text with poor contrast and tight leading can be very difficult to read for many people.
A very long line of text that extends beyond the recommended character limit of seventy-five characters per line can make reading difficult and tiring for users.
Good typography is invisible. Great typography speaks to the reader without ever being noticed. It carries meaning through form.

Every book you trust was set by people who knew what a sentence is. Your browser doesn’t. A working argument — with the browser default, text-wrap: pretty, and a compositor measured live on this page.

Good typography is often invisible. When it is done well, the reader's focus is drawn entirely to the content, rather than the formatting. However, when typography is poor, it creates friction, making it harder for the reader to absorb the information and resulting in a disjointed user experience.

Typography is the craft of endowing human language with a durable visual form, and thus with an independent existence. Its heartwood is calligraphy—the dance, on a smaller page, of the living, speaking hand—and its roots reach into living soil, though its branches may be hung with dead conventions.

The reader's comfort is not a luxury but a necessity. When text is set with care—when the spaces between letters breathe properly, when lines are neither cramped nor sprawling, when the eye can traverse a line without fatigue—reading becomes what it should be: transparent. The reader forgets the page and remembers the ideas.

Research in typography and human factors has given us concrete guidance. We know that line lengths between 45 and 75 characters optimize reading speed and comprehension. We understand that line height affects both legibility and aesthetic harmony. We have measured the impact of letter spacing on readers with visual impairments and dyslexia.

These are not arbitrary rules handed down by tradition. They are principles discovered through careful observation of how human eyes and brains process written language. When we set type according to evidence, we honor both the reader and the text.
Pure ethos: Roman inscriptional capitals — the letterforms of law courts and monuments. Authority with no warmth and no argument; it does not persuade, it decrees.
Pure pathos: a shout with a marker pen. No institution behind it, no system inside it — only feeling. Protest signs, emergencies, zines.
Pure logos: the voice of the machine itself. Every character the same width, feeling not included. Code, terminals, raw data.
Warm pathos: a note in a familiar hand. Where Permanent Marker shouts, Caveat confides — sympathy cards, marginalia, the human voice at whisper volume.
The friendly machine: slab warmth bolted onto a grid. Product docs that want to feel dependable rather than cold.
A literary serif engineered for screens — bookish credibility that survives a phone. Essays, longform, serious blogs.
The plain workhorse: says nothing so the content says everything. Forms, documentation, interfaces that should disappear.
Forty years after print solved it, the browser catches up. Knuth’s mathematics, Tschichold’s tolerances, Bringhurst’s measures — running live on every paragraph of this page.

Your browser does not know what a sentence is. It does not know that a thought should not snap in half, or that a word left alone on a line looks abandoned, because it is. It fills each line until the words run out, and calls that typography.

Anyone can license the same typefaces. The tell is the setting. A rag that breathes. A line that ends where the thought ends. A quotation mark hanging in the margin, because the eye wants edges, not excuses. For forty years the browser could not do this, so design teams shipped text they would never have signed in print. That era is over. Clean type is the quietest possible proof that your team knows what it is doing -- visible in a glance, impossible to fake.
Opening quotes hang their full glyph into the margin; optical capitals pull left. The block aligns to the eye, not the em box.
The compositor finishes holding two hundred candidate paragraphs and chooses the most musical rag — never merely the cheapest.
Word-space tolerances derived from the measured width of your font’s own lowercase i. No magic numbers anywhere in the system.
Every composed line is re-measured after render. If the browser disagrees, the engine steps back rather than ship an overflow.
